comment: The ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Three requirement register, as reviewed policy. tools/check-essential-eight.mjs judges it and runs as the second script of the docs-sync chain step. Harness-owned and sha-pinned by check-gate-integrity.mjs: widening a grade is a CODEOWNERS-reviewed act that appears in a PR diff.

READ THIS FIRST — WHAT THIS FILE DOES NOT CLAIM. A codebase cannot hold an Essential Eight maturity level and neither can a generator. Maturity attaches to an ORGANISATION’S SYSTEM; ASD operates no approved-product list and certifies nobody. Assessment is all-or-nothing per strategy AND per package, and risk-accepting one whole strategy forces Maturity Level Zero overall — so a repo-scoped ML3 claim does not merely overstate, it inverts. The Essential Eight also contains ZERO software-development controls (every ISM Guidelines-for-software-development control is tagged "Essential 8: N/A"). This register exists so that a generated application is never the BLOCKER to its operator’s assessment. It never claims the application IS ML3.

THE MODEL. 149 cumulative requirements (Appendix C of the 27 Nov 2023 model). A naive union of the appendices gives 152 and is WRONG — exactly three ML1/ML2 requirements are SUPERSEDED at ML3, and they are recorded in supersededAtML3[] rather than deleted, because a cut requirement and a forgotten requirement look identical six months later. Per-strategy counts are asserted by the gate: 13/16/23/29/19/11/27/11. WHAT THE CENSUS DOES NOT HOLD, stated because a reader could reasonably assume otherwise: it pins expectedCounts.total and byStrategy, and BOTH ARE INVARIANT UNDER A REGRADE. Changing an outcome from not-implemented to effective moves no strategy count, and flipping a row from the product boundary to the organisation boundary moves none either — a row stays in its strategy whatever it is graded. So the census catches a row LOST, DUPLICATED or MIS-ATTRIBUTED and catches nothing about whether a grade is deserved. That is deliberate (arithmetic cannot judge a grade) and it means the controls on grading are the ones in the GRADING IS CONSERVATIVE rules below, the canary closure, and CODEOWNERS review of this file's diff — never the count.

TWO FIELDS, DELIBERATELY. "reachability" is FROZEN from the research pass (design/research/essential-eight-ml3-research.json) and records what a codebase COULD satisfy. "outcome" is GRADED against this tree and records what actually ships. Collapsing them is how a register inflates: three Regular-backups rows are reachability "direct" and outcome "not-implemented", and that gap is the point of keeping both.

GRADING IS CONSERVATIVE, BY RULE. (1) "effective" needs a live control whose SUBJECT IS the requirement. (2) A requirement about an artefact this tree does not produce is "not-implemented", never "alternate-control" — absence is not a control. (3) "alternate-control" needs a shipped mechanism whose PURPOSE is the requirement’s intent, and always carries assessorMayRefuse, because an alternate control is demonstrated by the system owner and never pre-earned by a generator. (4) Where two grades are defensible the LOWER one is taken. (5) An artefact already claimed by another row is not claimed again — double-counting is the commonest form of compliance inflation.

BOUNDARY. "product" means this system answers for the row and "outcome" is required. "organisation" means the asset class exists but the operator configures and evidences it; "outcome" is null and "owner" is required. Where the asset class is ABSENT from the generated system the row is product/not-applicable carrying a negativeProof — never silence.

EVIDENCE TIERS ARE ASD’S OWN RANKING. The assessment process guide calls documentation and interviews POOR evidence and testing with simulated activity EXCELLENT. "simulated-activity" requires a canary in tests/canary/injections.json that injects the violation and watches the gate go red; "system-generated-artefact" is a gate reading a real artefact; "documentation" is the honest floor and must not be dressed up as more.

SHELF LIFE. ASD opened consultation on 2026-06-15 to replace the Essential Eight with an ISM-grounded Essentials series, citing the cloud gap explicitly — roughly 12 months to deprecation and 24 to retirement. The obligations row conformance-e8-retirement carries the date.

requirements.text: An automated method of asset discovery is used at least fortnightly to support the detection of assets for subsequent vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.proof: .github/workflows/osv-scan.yml job `sbom-inventory` — `pnpm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx --lockfile-only` emitted daily, then CONSUMED by tools/check-sbom.mjs, which closes the component set against pnpm-lock.yaml in BOTH directions; the artefact is uploaded only after it passes
requirements.note: ALTERNATE, NOT EFFECTIVE, and the frozen reachability is why: ASD's asset discovery means discovering ASSETS ACROSS AN ESTATE — hosts, endpoints, services someone stood up and forgot. A dependency inventory discovers no assets; it enumerates the software composition of one repository whose contents were never in doubt. What it genuinely does is the clause's stated PURPOSE — "to support the detection of assets for subsequent vulnerability scanning activities" — because it is the exact input scan-full is aimed at, and it is now proven COMPLETE rather than merely produced. That is the shape of an alternate control (rule 3), so it carries assessorMayRefuse and an assessor may well refuse it. Rule 4 applied: "effective" was defensible on the purpose clause alone, and where two grades are defensible the lower is taken. The job is (schedule-gated) on the daily cron. Emission ALONE would have been documentation-tier theatre — `pnpm sbom` is one line and cannot go red — so the grade rests entirely on the consumption half: an under-reporting inventory reds, an inventory of a DIFFERENT tree reds, and a zero-component emission is a hard failure rather than an empty set quietly matching an empty set.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner with an up-to-date vulnerability database is used for vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.proof: .github/workflows/osv-scan.yml job `scan-full` (OSV.dev advisory database, resolved per run) + tools/check-framework-floor.mjs
requirements.note: Subject match is exact: a scanner with a current vulnerability database is used. The job is (schedule-gated) — DAILY cron since 0.10.0, plus push and dispatch — so it is proven periodically, not per-commit; the diff-aware `scan-pr` lane is the per-commit half. Residue: it scans the dependency graph, not a network estate. RULE 5 DISCLOSURE: this row, PA-03 and PA-05 all rest on the ONE `scan-full` job. That is not the double-counting rule 5 forbids — ASD splits three genuinely different questions about one scanner (does it have a current database; is it run daily against online services; is it run fortnightly against other applications) and one lane can honestly answer all three — but it is stated here rather than left to be noticed, because a reader who sees one row cannot tell how much weight the lane is carrying. They are deliberately NOT a sharedClause: the clause TEXTS differ, so the machine closure cannot see the overlap and this sentence is the only place it is recorded.

requirements.text: Online services that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.
requirements.note: STILL UNBUILT, and the note this replaces was wrong about why. 0.9.9 built the end-of-life closure and it does NOT reach this row: a deprecation flag is registry metadata about a PACKAGE, and an online service has no such flag in any artefact this tree contains. requirements.text: Applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, Adobe Flash Player, and security products that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.
requirements.note: The npm dependency graph IS the application inventory for this system, and pnpm records the npm registry’s own `deprecated` message on a package entry at resolve time — so the vendor’s support statement is a committed third-party artefact here rather than a claim anyone in this repo wrote, which is what lets the check ride the per-commit chain without violating the hermeticity rule. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and why assessorMayRefuse is set: it DISPOSITIONS rather than REMOVES. ASD’s verb is "removed". A fresh scaffold resolves six vendor-deprecated packages; five are development-only and one (uuid@7, reached through expo -> @expo/config-plugins -> xcode) is inside the PRODUCTION dependency closure and is ACCEPTED with a re-review at 0.11.0, not removed — an assessor may reasonably decline to accept "dispositioned, scope-verified and expiring" as "removed", and that refusal is the honest reading of the text. Two further limits stated rather than discovered: the census is only as current as the last RESOLUTION (pnpm copies the flag in at resolve time, so a tree that never reinstalls holds a stale census — hence the 31-day review window and the scheduled lapse check) — and the 0.10.0 re-review DEMONSTRATED that limit rather than merely restating it: a fresh sweep of all 1539 resolved versions against the registry returned EIGHT deprecations where this register carries six, both extras production-scope, because the committed census was resolved earlier than the sweep. Neither extra became a row (their successors are in-range, undeprecated, and published before the previous tag), but a control that can be shown to lag is one whose review window is doing work. Third limit, unchanged: "in the production dependency closure" is NOT "in the shipped bundle" (bundling follows imports, a lockfile records dependencies), so the production grade is a ceiling on exposure and not a measurement of it.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users to their organisation’s online services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive data.
requirements.note: THE RAIL AND THE SURFACE NOW BOTH EXIST AND THIS ROW STILL DOES NOT PASS — the honest gap has narrowed to one word: MANDATORY. The database rail (supabase/migrations/20260812000000_mfa_aal2.sql) refuses aal1 reads for any user holding a verified factor, on every surface including one nobody wrote; since 1.0.0 the enrolment surface ships on both platforms — the offered TOTP step in web and mobile sign-up, the challenge screens, the security page and screen managing factors, all driving the one ceremony in packages/platform/supabase/src/mfa-flow.ts — so a user can enrol, verify and satisfy the rail end to end, proven by the vitest/RNTL suites beside each surface. What remains missing is USE for everyone: GoTrue carries no `required` field anywhere in its MFA configuration, so a user who declines the offered step still authenticates with one factor, and ASD's sentence says MFA IS USED, not that it is available. Condition row e8-mfa-mandatory-enrolment owns that residue. (ADR: docs/adr/20260812-mfa-aal2.md.)

A generator that shipped a per-table MFA register would be answering that question on the operator's behalf and getting it wrong for most of them. WHY THIS IS A BOUNDARY MOVE AND NOT A REGRADE: outcome goes to null, which is strictly LESS than the not-implemented it replaces — the register stops claiming anything here rather than claiming something better. The enrolment half is a separate and genuinely unreachable matter tracked at MFA-01/04/06 (GoTrue's MFAConfiguration carries no Required field); this row is only about which repositories the factor gates. tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs closes the rail's SHAPE wherever the operator applies it, never its coverage, and that is the correct division.

requirements.text: Successful and unsuccessful multi-factor authentication events are centrally logged.
requirements.note: Not for the reason this row first gave. GoTrue DOES record auth events — auth.audit_log_entries ships in every Supabase project — and the earlier note claiming nothing captures them was wrong. Verified against a running stack: a signup wrote `user_signedup`, a sign-in wrote `login`, and THREE failed sign-ins wrote NOTHING. The requirement says "successful AND unsuccessful", so the unsuccessful half has no record to forward, which is what fails it. Two further gaps, both verified: the table is not "central" (it lives in the same database as the system it records, so a database compromise takes the log with it), and reaching an off-platform sink needs a log drain, which is Dashboard-only on this platform. 0.10.0 SPLIT THE OWNER, because the two gaps are not the same kind of thing and one row could not be honest about both: the BUILDABLE half — the unsuccessful events that are written nowhere — is e8-auth-event-trail at 0.11.0, since an application-level trail into audit.events at the sign-in seam would capture what the platform drops, and audit.events already has the append-only discipline auth.audit_log_entries cannot be given. The CEILING half — 'centrally' — is e8-central-log-forwarding, and is not schedulable. This row names the buildable owner because that is the one a release can act on; building it alone does NOT pass this row, and that is the point of the split rather than a defect in it.

Every seat below 40 gets the genuine article (an ELEVATED owner runs revalidate_member); a lapsed owner revalidates THEMSELVES, gated on a verified second factor (aal2) rather than on a second person. An assessor may refuse self-revalidation as not being revalidation in ASD's sense, which is exactly what assessorMayRefuse records.

requirements.text: Privileged access events are centrally logged.
requirements.note: THE EVENTS EXIST AND ARE PROTECTED; WHAT IS MISSING IS "CENTRALLY". audit.events records this stream with the actor derived inside the writer, append-only in four layers, and supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql now proves the elevated role cannot read, forge, modify, delete or truncate it — attempted as service_role, not inferred from a grant lookup. What no part of this repository can do is FORWARD it: central logging means the record survives compromise of the system that produced it, and an in-database trail does not. The forwarding half is also asymmetric across the two platforms this stack deploys to, and deliberately not gated as though it were symmetric: one platform’s log drains are API- and Terraform-addressable, the other’s are Dashboard-only (verified negative against the live Management API specification, where `drain` appears only as an enum value and never as a path). A gate resolving either from a live endpoint is refused on this repository’s own hermeticity rule — a check that reads a third-party API turns an untouched commit red overnight, and this repo has paid for that once. Retention matters too: platform log retention tops out at 90 days by plan tier, so any requirement beyond that MUST ride a drain into a sink the operator controls. Obligation e8-central-log-forwarding.

requirements.text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.proof: supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql — 32 assertions against a running database. Append-only in four layers (no update/delete policy, no client grant, a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE row trigger that binds even a BYPASSRLS role, a BEFORE TRUNCATE statement trigger on the parent AND every partition), and, new in 0.9.9, the ELEVATED role ATTEMPTING each of read, forge, modify, delete and truncate rather than being inferred from a grant lookup — ASD ranks documentation POOR and simulated activity EXCELLENT, and a catalog read is closer to the first.
requirements.note: The ONE shared-clause instance whose subject stream actually exists: audit.events records privileged-access mutations, and its protection is proven by a suite that attempts the mutation and asserts refusal. The artefact is declared once in sharedClauses[] and claimed once, here. WHICH LAYER OWNS WHICH PROPERTY was established by experiment in 0.9.9: granting service_role USAGE and full DML reds exactly the READ and the FORGED INSERT and leaves UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE passing, because the triggers refuse those with every grant in place. So the grant is the sole control on reading and forging — which is why "just let the Edge Function read the audit table" is the single edit this suite exists to catch.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are performed and retained in accordance with business criticality and business continuity requirements.
requirements.timeframes: No fixed numeric window — frequency and retention are set by the organisation's own business criticality and business continuity requirements. ASD deliberately removed the previously prescriptive 'daily' frequency and 'three months or greater' retention; any checklist citing those numbers is pre-2023.
requirements.owner: organisation: business continuity plan supplying RPO/RTO and criticality classification
requirements.note: ASD deliberately REMOVED the prescriptive 'daily' frequency and 'three months or greater' retention in the 2023 model. Any checklist citing those numbers is pre-2023, and encoding them would gate a requirement ASD no longer makes. 0.9.9 SHIPPED THE EVIDENCE, not the determination. `tools/check-backup-posture.mjs` runs on a schedule (the `backup-evidence` job) and asks the platform whether this project actually has a recovery mechanism — Point-in-Time Recovery enabled, OR at least one completed daily backup. What it deliberately does NOT do is supply the number: tools/backup-posture.json ships `maxDailyBackupAgeHours` as NULL and reds when the lane is wired to a real project without it, because "in accordance with business criticality" is the operator's determination and a figure invented by a generator would be an obligation with no framework behind it. Two published facts to reason from, and no more: PITR carries a worst-case recovery point objective of two minutes, and NO RPO IS PUBLISHED FOR DAILY BACKUPS AT ALL — a blog sentence about losing "up to 24 hours worth of data" is a data-loss bound mentioned in passing, never a committed figure, and it does not appear in the documentation.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are synchronised to enable restoration to a common point in time.
requirements.note: Reachable and unbuilt. All three asset classes exist here (data = Postgres + Storage; applications = the built artefacts and their commit; settings = migrations, RLS, Edge Function source), but nothing emits an artefact binding them to one point in time. STILL UNBUILT, and 0.9.9 established precisely why the new lane does not move it. The `backup-evidence` job reports whether a recovery mechanism exists, which speaks to the DATA class and to a common point in time — PITR restores the database to any chosen second. It does not reach the other two classes this row names, because THE PLATFORM'S BACKUP DOES NOT CONTAIN THEM: Edge Functions, Auth settings and API keys, Realtime settings, extensions and project settings, read replicas and Storage API objects are all outside the database backup (the database holds only Storage metadata), and custom-role LOGIN passwords are stripped. The sharpest exclusion is the Vault/pgsodium root key: a backup carries ciphertext but not the key, so a restore into a new project cannot decrypt what it restored until the key is carried across by hand. So "synchronised to enable restoration to a common point in time" is true of the database and false of the system, and the lower grade is the honest one.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are retained in a secure and resilient manner.
requirements.note: Reachable and unbuilt. No backup object store, separate-account placement, envelope key or integrity check ships. installer/lib/rollback.mjs is HARNESS-INSTALL rollback (N=1, deleted by graduate) and is NOT application-data backup; counting it here would be the inflation this register exists to prevent. 0.9.9 recorded what the VENDOR attests, labelled as attestation rather than as anything this system demonstrates: backups are AES-256 encrypted at rest with keys protected by FIPS 140-2 validated HSMs, and are stored in S3 on infrastructure independent of the project's own resources. That is a contractual statement in the platform's data processing agreement, not an artefact any control here reads, so it cannot raise this grade — it is recorded so an assessor is told where the claim comes from and can weigh it. No storage region for backups is published. Whether daily backups aging past the plan retention window (7 / 14 / 30 days) are DELETED or merely made inaccessible is also unpublished: every statement is of the form "can access the last N days", which is an access statement and never a deletion one.

requirements.text: Restoration of data, applications and settings from backups to a common point in time is tested as part of disaster recovery exercises.
requirements.timeframes: The model text sets no interval; ASD's assessment process guide qualifies it as 'regular (at least annually) disaster recovery exercises', so at least annually is the assessor's working expectation.
requirements.owner: organisation: scheduled disaster recovery exercise, participants and after-action review
requirements.note: Restore-to-a-new-project (clone) is the non-destructive restore test and it is DASHBOARD-ONLY — all 115 paths of the live Supabase Management API OpenAPI spec were grepped for `clone` and returned zero.  ASD’s assessment process guide qualifies the interval as ‘regular (at least annually)’. TWO CORRECTIONS FROM 0.9.9's RE-VERIFICATION, both to claims this row previously made. FIRST, the clone finding is right but was stated imprecisely: the word `clone` DOES occur in the published schema — four times, every one of them a branch-pipeline step name (clone / pull / health / configure / migrate / seed / deploy) — and what is absent is a clone-to-a-new-project PATH. The absence is meaningful rather than merely unlisted, because the same schema publishes nine `x-internal` operations, so Supabase does expose endpoints it does not intend for general use. SECOND, "branching does not substitute because branches carry no data" IS WITHDRAWN AS A GRADED FACT. The branching guide does say new branches start with no data from the main project, but the CLI documents a `--with-data` flag ("Whether to clone production data to the branch database") and the Management API's own CreateBranchBody carries `with_data`. That is a contradiction between the vendor's own surfaces, and a register must not grade on either side of one. Also verified and worth stating: an in-place restore takes the project OFFLINE ("The project is inaccessible during this process") with no published downtime figure, and the vendor nowhere says a restore overwrites or destroys the existing database — so the case against a scheduled production restore drill is AVAILABILITY, which is quoted, not destruction, which is not. The `restore-point` endpoints are not a restore test either: they create a labelled rollback marker, BOTH operations are marked `x-internal`, and the only way to exercise one is the `undo` endpoint, which reverts the same project. Supabase publishes no disaster-recovery runbook and no RTO; the entire corpus offers one non-prescriptive sentence, on the clone page, recommending the operator "perform any necessary tests".

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) cannot access backups belonging to other user accounts.
requirements.owner: organisation: Supabase organisation role assignment
requirements.note: RECORDED AS UNSATISFIABLE BY THE PLATFORM, not as a gap in this harness. Supabase provides NO backup-administrator separation: `Developer` can restore (destructive), the only non-restoring role (`Read-Only`) requires Team plan or above, and no role grants backup-restore without broad project powers. An operator needing this separation has a plan floor, not a config option. 0.9.9 re-verified this against the raw permissions table rather than a rendering of it, and the finding holds in a sharper form. Supabase publishes exactly FOUR roles — Owner, Administrator, Developer, Read-Only — and the table grants Scheduled Backups only View / Download / Restore and PITR only View / Restore. `Developer` holds Download and Restore while being described as unable to change project settings, and `Read-Only`, the only role narrow enough to resemble a backup custodian, is denied both AND is gated behind Team or Enterprise — as are project-scoped role assignments at all. So there is no backup-administrator role to separate FROM: the requirement's subject does not exist on this platform. (A methodological note worth carrying, because it nearly produced a wrong answer: fetching that page through a summarising reader invented section headings the source does not contain and dropped the footnotes that carry the plan-gating facts. When the table cells ARE the evidence, read the raw markdown.)

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) are prevented from modifying and deleting backups.
requirements.owner: organisation: Supabase organisation role assignment and any external backup store IAM policy
requirements.note: Same platform finding as RB-07. Supabase also exposes no delete-backup permission at all — backups are destroyed only by destroying the project, which Owner and Administrator can do. 0.9.9 sharpened the delete finding and, in doing so, weakened it honestly. No Delete or Modify action for a backup appears anywhere — not as a row in the permissions table, and not as any method across all 115 published API paths. But THAT IS AN ABSENCE OF SURFACE, NOT A PUBLISHED CONTROL: Supabase nowhere states that backups cannot be deleted, it simply never offers the verb, and the register's own rule is that absence of a surface is never a control. The two documented pages also contradict each other on what deleting a PROJECT does to its backups — one says they are permanently removed from S3, the other that they become inaccessible.

requirements.text: Backup administrator accounts are prevented from modifying and deleting backups during their retention period.
requirements.timeframes: 'during their retention period' — the window is the organisation's own documented retention period set under RB-01, not an ASD-specified number. Deletion is permitted once that period has been exceeded.
requirements.note: Reachable ONLY for self-produced off-platform dumps under S3 Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode, which binds every principal including the account root. NOT satisfiable for Supabase-managed PITR — and since every project on PG >= 15.8.1.079 uses physical backups there is no downloadable backup artefact, so the only off-site copy is one the operator produces. REINFORCED BY 0.9.9 rather than moved, and this row is where the register's second grading rule does its clearest work. It is tempting to read "no role can delete a backup, and no API method exists to delete one" as satisfying a requirement that backup administrators be PREVENTED from deleting backups — and that reading would be wrong. Prevention is a control; an unoffered verb is a gap in the interface. No page publishes an immutability, WORM or object-lock guarantee for the buckets holding Supabase backups (searched: the backups guide, product security, the SOC 2 and HIPAA pages, the shared-responsibility model and the PITR usage page), so nothing here is being prevented from anything — it is merely not currently possible through the surfaces on offer, which is a different and weaker fact. One live gap is recorded as explicitly UNVERIFIABLE and must not be graded in either direction: whether reducing the PITR recovery retention period, or removing the PITR add-on, destroys backup data already inside the previous window. The vendor documents the billing consequence of removal and says the recovery period "can be changed if needed", and publishes no data-lifecycle statement at all. That is the most plausible undocumented path by which a privileged account could destroy backups during their retention period, and it is precisely the thing this requirement asks about.
